opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is to accept that, most of the time, you genuinely won't know. When you're early, especially building something at the frontier, the information you'd need to be sure simply doesn't exist yet. So the question isn't really "how do I know I'm right," it's "how do I make good decisions under uncertainty, and how do I find out quickly when I'm wrong."

A few things have helped me think about it.

First, separate reversible decisions from irreversible ones. Most decisions a young founder makes are actually two-way doors: which feature to try, which customer segment to talk to first, how to phrase the pitch. For those, speed matters far more than precision. You make the call, you watch what happens, and you adjust. The danger is treating every small decision with the gravity of a one-way door, because then you move too slowly and learn nothing. For the truly irreversible ones, like who your co-founder is, who you take money from, or what core technical bet the company rests on, it's worth slowing down, gathering more input, and sitting with it.

Second, write down why you're making the decision before you know the outcome. It sounds simple, but it's very powerful. Later, when the result comes in, you can tell whether you were right for the right reasons, right by luck, or wrong because your reasoning was flawed versus wrong because the world was just noisy. Without that record, you tend to rewrite history in your head, and you don't actually improve your judgment.

Third, find people who will tell you you're wrong. When you're young and things are moving fast, it's easy to surround yourself with people who are excited about what you're doing. That feels good, but it doesn't help you calibrate. I try to seek out people who have deep expertise and no reason to flatter me, and ask them specifically, "What would make this fail?"

And finally, I'd say conviction and humility aren't opposites. You need enough conviction to commit fully. Half-hearted execution gives you no signal, because if it fails you don't know whether the idea was bad or you just didn't really try. But you hold that conviction alongside a real willingness to update. The founders I admire most can say, "I believed this strongly, I tested it seriously, and the evidence says I was wrong, so we're changing course," without feeling that their identity is on the line.

So in a way, I don't think the goal is to always be right. The goal is to be wrong cheaply, learn fast, and make sure the few decisions that really matter get the care they deserve.

r001.rationale: The response says the information needed for certainty may not exist yet, but it does not state that waiting for more information may fail to improve a decision’s correctness.

r002.rationale: It recommends making decisions under uncertainty, especially for reversible choices: decide, observe what happens, and adjust.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of the time you genuinely cannot tell, and the mistake is waiting until you can. When I was starting Axiom, I had this instinct from academia that you should gather enough evidence before committing to a position. That works for a proof. It does not work for a company, because the information you need usually only appears after you act.

So the first thing I would say is to separate decisions by how reversible they are. If something can be undone in a few weeks, just decide. Pick the option you lean toward, write down why you picked it, and move. The cost of being wrong is small and the cost of deliberating is often larger than people realize, because the whole team is waiting on you. If a decision is hard to reverse, like who you bring on as a cofounder, what problem you fundamentally work on, or how you structure your cap table, then it deserves real time and you should talk to people who have been through it.

The second thing is to pay attention to what you actually believe versus what you think you are supposed to believe. A lot of young founders, myself included, absorb a lot of advice from investors and from Twitter and from more experienced people, and that advice is often correct on average but wrong for your specific situation. When I felt confused, it was usually because there was a gap between the consensus view and something I had observed directly. In those cases I have learned to trust the direct observation more, even if I cannot fully articulate why yet.

And the third thing is that being wrong is not the real risk. The real risk is being wrong slowly and not noticing. So I try to attach a test to every uncertain decision. If we go this direction, what should we see in a month or two if it is working, and what would tell us it is not? Then you are not deciding right or wrong in the moment. You are just making a bet and setting up a way to learn from it. Over time the quality of your judgment improves not because you get smarter, but because you have run many more of these experiments than someone who sat and waited for certainty.

r001.rationale: The response says that waiting for enough evidence is a mistake because the information founders need often appears only after they act.

r002.rationale: It advises founders to make reversible decisions promptly and to treat uncertain choices as bets with tests, rather than waiting for certainty.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to ask, “What would I need to learn to change my mind?” When you’re making a decision under uncertainty, you may not be able to know whether you’re right, but you can be clear about your assumptions and how you’ll test them.

I’d also distinguish between decisions you can reverse and decisions that are hard to undo. If you can reverse it, make a small bet, get feedback, and adjust. If it’s hard to undo, spend more time understanding the downside and seek out people who disagree with you.

The tricky part is that a good decision can still have a bad outcome. So you want to learn from what happens without treating every setback as proof that your judgment was wrong. Be willing to act, and equally willing to update.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges uncertainty and recommends testing assumptions, but does not say that waiting for more information may fail to make a decision more correct.

r002.rationale: It recommends making a small bet and acting under uncertainty, which communicates committing before knowing whether the decision is right.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is to ask, “Do I need to be right about this now, or can I learn my way toward an answer?” As a founder, you’re often making decisions before you have enough information. Waiting for certainty is itself a decision, and it has a cost.

So I would separate decisions that are easy to reverse from decisions that are hard to reverse. For something reversible, make a small bet, decide what evidence would change your mind, and get feedback quickly. For something harder to undo, take more time, seek out people who disagree with you, and understand what happens if you’re wrong.

And try to separate your identity from your hypothesis. You can be deeply committed to solving a problem without being attached to your first solution. The goal is to make a thoughtful decision with the information you have, then stay willing to update.

r001.rationale: The response says waiting for certainty has a cost, but does not clearly state that waiting for more information may fail to make the decision more correct.

r002.rationale: It recommends making a small bet on reversible decisions and making a thoughtful decision with the information available, while remaining willing to update.
